bio: My name is Vicente Hernaiz Santamaria. I was born in 1998 in Valladolid, Spain, and I'm currently living in Atlanta, USA. Design is in my DNA, my father has 40 years of experience as a graphic designer, my whole family works in creative fields, and I started learning Illustrator and Photoshop at 12. By 15 I was already doing entrepreneurial work in design. I went to high school in the science track, then studied Mechanical Engineering at the University of Valladolid for two years, covering 3 advanced mathematics courses, object-oriented coding and C++, business and economics, 3 physics courses, technical drawing, material science, and material resistance. I left to become a professional cyclist competing across Europe for teams including Eolo-Kometa (the Alberto Contador team) and Radio Popular Boavista, while simultaneously taking graphic design courses and keeping creative projects running in parallel. When a cycling contract didn't come through in 2023, I went all-in on design for about a year as a freelancer, branding, car wraps (I genuinely love car wrapping design), websites, packaging, prints, and 3D printing pieces. It was during this time I met my mentor and friend Jorge Jimenez Rolo, SEO, CRO and Behavioral manager and one of the leading SEO voices in the Spanish-speaking industry. What started as a project we collaborated on became an ongoing two-year mentorship. He opened my eyes to the data side of design and I was instantly hooked on UX. I was already deep into the Google UX Professional Certificate and Bootcamps in SEO and CRO when the SCAD cycling team coach reached out and offered me an athletic scholarship to study and race for the team. I said yes immediately. I'm now at SCAD's Atlanta campus studying BFA in UX Design, still competing as a sponsored cyclist, and obsessed with building things that work, for users and for business.

projects.description: End-to-end launch for a premium physiotherapy clinic in central Valladolid, Spain. projects.name: Beloo, Cycling Safety App
projects.description: Full UX engagement for Beloo, a cycling safety app that broadcasts a rider's position to emergency contacts, triggers incident alerts, and integrates roadside insurance. The brief: low daily usage, monetisation was unclear, and the app wasn't sticky. Four phases delivered end to end. Phase 1, full heuristic/UX audit surfacing inverted visual hierarchy, emotional disconnect, accessibility failures, IA gaps, and an aggressive yellow/orange palette without functional purpose. Phase 2, in-person user testing in Calpe, Spain, with pro and casual riders (including Spanish champion Ivan Romeo), week-long field use, Typeform surveys, and focus groups. Phase 3, interaction redesign built around an intelligent reminder system (smart ride timing, movement detection at 21–37 km/h, social proximity, morning motivation), widgets and shortcuts for one-tap ride start (not five), and integrations with Strava, TrainingPeaks, Suunto, Apple Watch, and Garmin Edge. Phase 4, complete IA and UI rebuild: five-module sitemap (home with AI sphere, social, map, you, premium), glove-friendly tap targets, a 3D Spline AI sphere as the primary interaction element (amber = standby, blue-green = broadcasting), typewriter-animated real-time feedback, rewards, and a clearer premium tier. Preliminary follow-up testing with target users suggests an estimated 60-70% increase in repeat usage; Vicente labels this an estimate, not an instrumented result, and says so if asked.

projects.name: Housing Help × Deloitte
projects.client: HUD Atlanta Regional Office, via Deloitte Digital. HUD (U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development) is the federal agency that funds and regulates affordable housing; the Atlanta office oversees 8 southeastern states.

ux_team: Vicente Hernáiz, Prototyping & Design Systems Lead

projects.description: AI-powered mobile platform that streamlines government housing inspections under the new NSPIRE federal framework, designed for three user roles (tenants, landlords, inspectors) and for national scale. Vicente led the prototyping and owned the design system from day one (intentionally decoupled from branding, which saved weeks of rework). He defined the AI interaction model built on the principle 'AI advises, humans decide', with three AI functions: Documentation Assistant (real-time photo/lighting/angle guidance), Metric Interpreter (plain-language translation of regulatory text), and Compliance Decision Support (predicting violations from historical patterns). Resolved a mid-project branding deadlock with a role-based colour strategy (green for tenants, teal-blue for landlords, blue-purple for inspectors) that the branding team adopted as the foundation for the full visual identity. Visual language: glass morphism adapted for compliance context, tuned for accessibility. Hit WCAG AAA (federal requirement), validated against low-vision and colour-blindness conditions. Core platform value prop: the 24-hour NSPIRE compliance window for life-threatening deficiencies. Usability testing simplified the tenant reporting flow from 10 steps with decision branches to a linear 7-step flow (open → report → photo → notes → AI analyses → AI generates → send). Device-first by role: phone for tenants, tablet for inspectors, tablet/desktop for landlords. Validated by Google Design experts Russell Matsuo (UX Lead), Roque Silva (Product Design), and Mike Buzzard (Design Systems), plus Deloitte stakeholders.

projects.name: Uber Eats, Conditions Shaping Robotic Food Delivery (IDUS 215 Contextual Research)
projects.description: A ten-week contextual research engagement on the friction, perception and ideal experience of robotic last-mile food delivery, framed around the Uber Eats / Serve Robotics partnership. Central question: what does it take for a robotic delivery experience to be adopted with confidence by users, human couriers and restaurants? As Team-Lead Vicente owned research planning, fieldwork distribution, synthesis sessions, quality control on the final deliverable, and the decision to ship the deliverable as an interactive web client book instead of a static PDF. Five macro phases: research planning, contextual fieldwork & cultural probes, affinity diagram & synthesis, an Ideal Experience Framework using the Lextant method, and recommendations for Uber Eats.
projects.innovation: Introduced 'web client books' as the project deliverable format, replacing the traditional 80-page static PDF with an interactive Next.js site built with Claude Code and hosted on Vercel. Supports progressive disclosure, lateral navigation, live framework embeds, and stays as a living reference for the client team rather than a document filed after one meeting.

methodology.framework: Lextant Framework, a generative research methodology developed by the consultancy Lextant for translating emotional user insight into design opportunity. We used it as the spine of the analysis: raw observations from every interview, probe and intercept were translated into desired-experience statements grouped by four emotional pillars.

methods.name: Cultural Probes

methods.name: Affinity Synthesis
methods.detail: every insight had to triangulate across at least two methods to earn a place in the synthesis

pre_order_transparency_gap: Users can't find a clear way to order with a robot. No participant located a path in the Uber Eats app to specifically request robot delivery; some abandoned, others received it without asking
No transparency in the food-ordering process, the system feels like a black box (restaurant selection, delivery type, contingencies)
Robots all look alike, brand identity collapses on the sidewalk; users can't tell Uber/Serve units from DoorDash, Kiwibot or Starship
Users feel they can't choose and have no control over delivery format changes
city_and_environment: Weather is a constraint that worries users. Rain, snow, low visibility are the norm for half the country; system fails silently to the user, who only sees a delay
The sidewalk reality includes broken curb cuts, debris, unmapped obstacles, parked scooters; robots inherit every infrastructure flaw

The city isn't ready. Robotic delivery presupposes an infrastructure layer (predictable curb access, elevator integration, electricity at staging, network coverage past the last mile) that doesn't exist yet
Robots aren't enough. Peak-hour ceilings mean the robotic fleet can't absorb high-demand volume, so traditional couriers re-enter the loop. Robotic delivery is a supplement, not a substitute
emotional_gap_at_handoff: Impersonal hand-off. The robot opens, the user takes the bag, nothing is said, nothing is felt. The system reaches peak emotional contact at the same instant it's most silent. Quote: 'It just opens. Nothing happens.'
Human vs robotic. Robots gain speed and predictability but lose the micro-moments of social value (smile, confirmation, sense someone tried). Robotic neutrality reads as indifference
silent_trust_signals: Unlock-on-arrival is the single moment that decides trust. All previous friction is forgiven or condemned in the two-second moment the user opens the robot
Food quality on arrival is the loudest silent signal. Hot, intact food forgives almost every upstream friction; bad food cannot be recovered by UI

projects.name: Radioactive Car Wrapping, Peugeot RCZ
projects.description: Full vinyl wrap for a widebody Peugeot RCZ (custom bodykit + rear spoiler) with a post-nuclear / post-apocalyptic aesthetic. The client wanted rust, radiation, graffiti, and decay, all evoking the visual language of a world that had already ended. Process: (1) panel measurement and texture-direction planning in Illustrator, vector graffiti and radiation zone layout; (2) view-by-view composition in Photoshop using mesh-warp to adapt textures to body panel directions, extensive manual anti-tiling work to eliminate visible repetition at print scale; (3) hand-drawn graphic elements painted on Wacom tablet directly in Photoshop, including radiation symbols, graffiti tags, paint drips, stencilled lettering, all hand-applied for authentic imperfection; (4) print layout optimised to 1.5 m × 17 m from a 1.5 m × 25 m available roll, saving 8 linear metres of premium vinyl; (5) printed on HP Latex 730, laminated, cut on external plotter; (6) panel-by-panel installation with heat gun and squeegee over widebody compound curves. Total: 65 hours design and print prep, 55 hours installation, 120 hours total.

projects.name: Centre Point Global, School Travel Platform
projects.role: Product & UX Lead, freelance (client: Jorge J. Rolo, business & engineering)
projects.duration: Ongoing since June 2026, Phase 1 (MVP) in build
projects.description: Centre Point Global is a real, family-run school-travel agency in Madrid run by Jorge J. Rolo. Their entire online presence was a single static WordPress page: not indexable, no CMS, no online payment. Vicente was hired as a freelance Product & UX Lead to turn it into a platform. Phase 1 (MVP) scopes three capabilities: an SEO-optimised, dynamic trip catalogue with its own page per trip and category; a self-serve CMS so the operations team can publish without a developer; and Stripe Payment Links so families can pay a deposit or the full amount in two clicks. Process: (1) stakeholder mapping (Mendelow power/interest matrix) across the B2B2C chain, coordinating teacher, school leadership, paying family, before deriving any persona; (2) an 11-competitor heuristic audit (Nielsen heuristics, verified reviews) identifying that no competitor combines transparent pricing, full online payment, and real-time family tracking; (3) UX and conversion research grounded in NN/g and Baymard evidence (checkout field counts, hidden-cost abandonment, filter design); (4) a WCAG 2.1 AA colour audit of the brand palette that caught coral and magenta failing as text (3.42:1 and 3.73:1 against a 4.5:1 minimum) and defined AA-safe -700 variants plus a 60-30-10 usage rule, flagged P0 before any token shipped; (5) an 11-template information architecture and keyword-scored SEO roadmap (local Madrid landing pages as the Phase 1 engine); (6) an agentic build in Claude Code, an orchestrator session directing ephemeral specialist sub-agents (SEO, frontend/design system, CRO, accessibility, CMS/data, QA), each deliverable reviewed and verified before acceptance. The project is openly in development: Phase 2 (institutional/split payment, role-based panels, nationwide SEO, editorial CMS, Stripe Connect) is scoped but not started, and several items (final logo assets, legal pages, full palette migration, real user testing) are explicitly still open.

projects.name: AERO2, Performance Nasal Strips
projects.description: AERO2 is a European performance nasal strip brand for high-intensity cycling. The brand arrived with an existing wordmark; Vicente retouched and refined it into a production-ready lockup paired with a die-cut "bone" icon mark, then led a color psychology study to decide the brand's launch color. Process: (1) positioning workshop locking the brand as inspirational, premium performance, built to be noticed racing more than training; (2) five candidate colorways (R1 Volt Green, R2 Cobalt Blue, R3 Periwinkle, R4 Navy, R5 Yellow/Oxblood) shortlisted from color-psychology reasoning and cross-cultural color-preference research; (3) mixed-method testing, printed color comparisons and in-person interviews with cyclists, runners and triathletes, plus a written survey (32 respondents, Google Forms) collecting word associations and a 1–5 purchase-likelihood rating per color; (4) Volt Green selected as the hero SKU (highest word-association match on "engineered performance", zero collision with World Tour team colors); (5) one packaging dieline (resealable stand-up pouch) engineered to carry all five colorways without changing layout, with full production files (color specs, barcode, QR, CE/lot/expiry marks); (6) roadmap for the next two SKUs derived directly from the research, Cobalt Blue for affordable everyday training and Periwinkle/White for rest-and-recovery.

faq.q: Tell me more about the Uber Eats robotic food delivery project.
faq.a: Ten-week contextual research engagement (IDUS 215, Spring 2026) on the conditions shaping robotic last-mile food delivery in the United States, framed around the Uber Eats and Serve Robotics partnership. I was Team-Lead: I owned research planning, fieldwork distribution, synthesis sessions, and quality control on the final deliverable. Five macro phases: research planning → contextual fieldwork & cultural probes → affinity diagram & synthesis → an Ideal Experience Framework using the Lextant method → recommendations for Uber Eats. I also made the call to ship the deliverable as an interactive web client book instead of a static PDF, built with Claude Code on Next.js and hosted on Vercel. Case study: vicentehernaiz.tech/projects/uber-eats. Live client book: idus-215-uber-robots-research.vercel.app

faq.q: What research methods did you use on the Uber Eats project?
faq.a: Six complementary methods, triangulated so every insight had to land in at least two before it earned a place in the synthesis: (1) online & desk research (market, players, regulation), (2) cultural probes with two participants (Camille & Hampton) over five days using video diaries, photo prompts and reflective journaling, (3) six in-depth customer interviews, (4) six restaurant interviews across Real Tacos, Ponko Chicken, Shake Shack, Subway and Sweetgreen, (5) sensory intercepts on the Georgia Tech campus, (6) affinity synthesis that fed directly into a Lextant Framework. Diagram and protocols live in the case study at vicentehernaiz.tech/projects/uber-eats

faq.q: What is the Lextant framework and why did you use it?
faq.a: The Lextant Framework is a generative research methodology developed by the consultancy Lextant for translating emotional user insight into design opportunity. We used it as the spine of our Uber Eats analysis: raw observations from every interview, probe and intercept were translated into 'desired-experience statements' grouped by four emotional pillars (Peace of mind, Connection, Confidence, and Delight). Each pillar becomes a target the design must reach. The output is a populated framework that holds the project's entire research conclusion in a single view: what users feel today, what they should feel in the ideal, and the design moves that bridge the two. Static snapshot is in the case study; interactive version is at idus-215-uber-robots-research.vercel.app/ideal-experience

faq.q: What were the key findings of the Uber Eats research?
faq.a: The findings cluster in four themes. (1) Pre-order transparency gap: users can't find a clear way to order with a robot in the Uber Eats app, the food-ordering process feels like a black box, robots all look alike so branding collapses on the sidewalk, and users feel they have no control when the delivery format changes. (2) City & environment: weather worries users (the system fails silently), the sidewalk reality (curb cuts, debris, unmapped obstacles), the city isn't ready (no predictable infrastructure layer), and robots aren't enough, since the fleet doesn't scale to peak demand. (3) The emotional gap at hand-off: 'it just opens, nothing happens', and robotic neutrality reads as indifference; human couriers gain warmth that robots strip away. (4) Silent trust signals: unlock-on-arrival is the single moment that decides trust, and food quality on arrival is the loudest silent signal, since hot intact food forgives almost every upstream friction. The full set lives in the web client book at idus-215-uber-robots-research.vercel.app

faq.q: Tell me about the cultural probes work on the Uber Eats project.
faq.a: Two participants documented their delivery experience over five days through video diaries, photo prompts and short reflective journaling. Cultural probes surface the *quiet* friction that surveys and interviews miss: the unspoken half-second of hesitation before unlocking the robot, the small disappointments that don't make it into a survey because they're below the threshold of complaint. The probe outputs (videos + screenshots) are embedded in the case study at vicentehernaiz.tech/projects/uber-eats and informed the emotional-gap and silent-trust-signal findings.

Restaurant interviews covered Real Tacos Beltline, Real Tacos Midtown, Ponko Chicken Midtown, Shake Shack Piedmont Park, Subway Georgia Tech and Sweetgreen Tech Square. Sensory intercepts were conducted on the Georgia Tech campus where Serve Robotics units operate. Customer interviews and cultural probes spanned a broader Atlanta participant pool.

faq.q: What is a 'web client book' and why did you build one?
faq.a: Web client books are a new deliverable format I introduced on the Uber Eats research project to replace the traditional 80-page static PDF. A PDF delivers information but doesn't communicate it well, eighty linear pages are a wall. A web client book lets you structure information for progressive disclosure (the client enters at the level they need), supports lateral navigation and anchored sections, and embeds live interactivity, framework previews, transitions, and quotes in context. It's built with Next.js, developed with Claude Code, and deployed on Vercel. The client gets a living reference they can come back to and share with their team, not a document that gets filed after one meeting. See it live at idus-215-uber-robots-research.vercel.app

faq.q: Tell me more about the Radioactive Car Wrapping project.
faq.a: February 2024 client project, solo, 120 hours total. Full vinyl wrap for a widebody Peugeot RCZ (custom bodykit and rear spoiler) with a post-nuclear / post-apocalyptic aesthetic, the client wanted rust, radiation, graffiti, and decay. I planned every panel and the texture-flow direction in Illustrator so the graphics survived stretch and bend during install, then composed each view in Photoshop with mesh-warp and a long manual anti-tiling pass so the textures looked organic rather than repeated. All graphic elements (radiation symbols, graffiti tags, paint drips, stencil lettering) were hand-drawn on Wacom tablet. I optimised the print layout to 1.5 × 17 m from a 1.5 × 25 m available roll (8 linear metres of premium vinyl saved), printed on HP Latex 730, laminated, plotter-cut, and installed panel by panel: 65 h design + print prep, 55 h installation.
